pinterest.title: Serbian Wedding Traditions: 10 Customs in the Order They Happen
pinterest.description: Serbian wedding traditions make far more sense seen in order: the prosidba to ask for the bride's hand, the svatovi collecting her behind the barjak, a Serbian Orthodox service with rings, crowns and a shared cup, then the welcome at her new home and the kolo. Our guide separates what the Church sets from what families keep, for Serbian-Australian couples planning in Serbia or at home.

pinterest.title: The Kum at a Serbian Wedding: Far More Than a Best Man
pinterest.description: At a Serbian Orthodox wedding the kum is the first of two church witnesses, with the stari svat. He exchanges the rings during the betrothal and holds the couple's candles until the service ends. Families often speak of kumstvo as a bond that lasts well beyond the day. Choose your kum early: some churches ask for his church baptism certificate too.

pinterest.title: Serbian Orthodox Wedding Crowns, the Common Cup and the Walk Around the Table
pinterest.description: Inside a Serbian Orthodox wedding: the couple's right hands are bound with a white cloth, crowns are placed on their heads and they share red wine in three sips. The priest then leads them three times around the table. The service is called venčanje, from venac, a wreath. Requirements differ between parishes, so ask your parish priest.

slides: Serbian wedding traditions you did not know, in the order they happen
1. The prosidba: the visit to ask for the bride's hand opens the sequence. A family occasion first.
2. The kum: the first of two church witnesses. He exchanges the rings and holds the couple's candles. Far more than a best man.
3. The barjak: the svatovi set out to collect the bride, traditionally with the wedding flag leading the way. Then her family makes them "buy" her back. Theatre, not commerce.
4. The apple: as it is often told, an apple is set high and the groom or his party tries to hit it before the bride is led out. Details vary from family to family.
5. The church: rings, crowns, a white cloth binding right hands, a shared cup of red wine and a threefold walk around the table.
6. The kolo: a circle dance inscribed by UNESCO for Serbia in 2017. Learnt mainly by joining in.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A Serbian wedding is less a single ceremony than a sequence: a visit to ask for the bride's hand, a party sent to collect her, a church service with crowns and a shared cup, and a welcome at her new home.

Seen in order, the customs make far more sense. The church rite is set by the Serbian Orthodox Church. The folk customs around it belong to families, and no two families keep them in quite the same way.

Which customs does your family keep? Tell us in the comments.
